item.title: Kratom-labeled Products in the US Compared With Traditionally Consumed Natural Kratom in Southeast Asia
item.description:
Kratom-labeled products consumed in the United States and natural kratom consumed in Southeast Asia (SEA) are very different in their chemistry and safety profiles. Water-based decoction, frequently consumed in SEA, is prepared using freshly harvested, not dried leaves of Mitragyna speciosa tree, indigenous to the SEA region. Our research demonstrates that the decoction contains mitragynine and its congeners in organic, water-soluble salts form, not in the pure base alkaloids form. In addition, our preliminary evaluation has not detected 7-hydroxymitragynine, a highly potent oxidative derivative of mitragynine, in the decoction prepared from the freshly harvested and unprocessed leaves. The differences in the products' chemistry may be responsible for the observed differences in safety profiles between the products consumed in the United States and in the SEA countries. Kratom-labeled products in the United States are sold under the false promises that they reflect the natural kratom products consumed in SEA. Consumers of these products and health care practitioners in the United States may not be aware that the natural kratom products traditionally consumed in SEA (ie, freshly harvested unprocessed whole leaves and a water-based decoction prepared from such leaves) have different chemistry and are consumed differently than the US products, including kratom-leaf-derived US products (ie, capsules, powders, or tea bags claiming to contain dried natural kratom leaves), as well as the highly concentrated or semisynthetic products. The traditional natural products consumed in the SEA countries may also have a different safety profile and pharmacological effects.

Karunakaran T, Vicknasingam K, Chawarski MC

item.title: Identifying Subtypes of Cannabis Use Disorder: A Latent Class Analysis Among Daily Cannabis Consumers and Associated Sociodemographic and Cannabis Characteristics
item.description:
Background: Cannabis use disorder (CUD) is relatively common among daily cannabis consumers; however, no studies have explored subtypes of CUD based on updated DSM-5 CUD criteria among daily consumers. Our study fills this gap and explores differences between subtypes in sociodemographic and cannabis correlates.

Methods: US adults aged 18 years or older were recruited from social media (February to April 2022) to complete an online survey including sociodemographic characteristics (e.g., age, sex, reason for cannabis use), cannabis use behaviors, and DSM-5 CUD criteria. Latent class analyses (LCA) identified classes of individuals based on endorsement of CUD criteria. Differences in sociodemographic and cannabis characteristics were explored with bivariate testing.

Results: Data from N=4140 daily consumers were analyzed. A 5-class model was selected and labeled as (1) Minimal Problems (30%; no CUD [0-1 criteria]), (2) Common Problems (45%; mild CUD [2-3 criteria]), (3) Social, Physical, and Emotional Problems (6.6%; mild-moderate CUD [2-5 criteria] including use despite physical/emotional and social problems), (4) Physical Dependence Problems (16%; moderate-severe CUD [4+ criteria] including tolerance/withdrawal), and (5) Severe Problems (3.1%; severe CUD [6+ criteria]). Sociodemographic differences between classes included age and reasons for use (P≤0.001). Cannabis correlates (i.e., frequency, quantity) mainly differentiated the Minimal Problems class from others.

Conclusions: Among daily cannabis consumers, strategies to limit use throughout the day, driving under the influence and coping with cravings are warranted. Interventions for moderate CUD should be tailored for psychological/interpersonal versus physiological problems, while those with severe CUD would benefit from interventions to target global problems.

Struble CA, Alschuler D, Wall M, Hasin DS, Borodovsky JT, Aharonovich E

item.title: Visiting Nurse Services-facilitated Outpatient Low-dose Buprenorphine Initiation and Engagement in Severe Mental Illness and Ongoing Fentanyl Use: A Case Report
item.description:
Background and objectives: Outpatient low-dose buprenorphine initiation (LDBI) is challenging for individuals with severe mental illness and poor treatment adherence. Visiting nurse services (VNS) may support LDBI in these complex patients.

Methods: We present a 64-year-old male with opioid use disorder, schizoaffective disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder who underwent outpatient LDBI supported by VNS.

Results: VNS managed medication administration and adherence monitoring, facilitating successful LDBI and sustained engagement.

Discussion and conclusions: VNS facilitated outpatient LDBI and buprenorphine treatment engagement in a patient with fluctuating psychiatric illness and ongoing fentanyl use.

Scientific significance: This case suggests that VNS may facilitate outpatient LDBI and engagement among clinically complex patients in the fentanyl era.

Arbelo Cruz F, Castillo JC, Pérez Palmer N

item.title: Scoping Review of Implementation Science in Digital Intervention Research for Substance Use Disorders
item.description:
Objectives: Digital substance use interventions (DSUI) have demonstrated effectiveness in preventing, treating, and supporting recovery of substance use disorders (SUD), but their large-scale adoption and sustained implementation remain limited. To highlight the state of the science for DSUI implementation research, we conducted a scoping review of relevant studies of implementation of DSUI.

Methods: We used Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses - Scoping Review guidelines. Search was conducted using keywords (eg, technology, substance use, implementation) in Medline, PsycINFO, and Health Technology Assessment databases. Studies without implementation data, protocols, reviews, editorials, and non-English papers were excluded. Publications were included through February 2023. We screened 4178 abstracts and 148 full texts using Covidence software. We extracted implementation-related data from the included studies and organized it using standardized terminology for implementation determinants, strategies, and outcomes.

Results: The 48 studies represented implementation (n=7), determinant (n=8), and combined effectiveness and implementation studies or hybrid studies (n=33). Most common DSUI were treatment and recovery support approaches for general drug use, most frequently delivered as electronic programs on computers. Only 12 of 48 studies used implementation frameworks. Implementation strategies were rarely described. Acceptability was the most evaluated implementation outcome (n=26), and no study evaluated implementation costs. Evaluation of patient-level implementation determinants and longer-term sustainment outcomes was lacking.

Conclusions: To accelerate translation and improve research rigor, future DSUI research should systematically apply implementation science frameworks to evaluate implementation determinants (including patient-level), document and test implementation strategies, and evaluate outcomes, including fidelity, cost, and sustainment.

Rao D, Clement MK, Reardon CM, Saldana L, Campbell ANC, Lord SE
